one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary detectors are effectively closed-vocabulary: novel-class success is concentrated on concepts frequent in web caption pretraining, and performance on genuinely caption-rare concepts collapses.
Open-vocabulary detection AP is a property of the query vocabulary list, not the detector: adding or removing distractor class names materially changes scores and method rankings.

Open-vocabulary detectors lack a calibrated none-of-the-above: their scores cannot express that a region matches no queried concept, causing systematic false positives when the true object is outside the vocabulary.
Multi-word and rare-phrase query degradation in open-vocabulary detection is largely a text-side tokenization and phrase-composition artifact, not a visual difficulty effect.
Open-vocabulary detectors are context classifiers in disguise: pasting objects into atypical scenes collapses their naming accuracy far more than it collapses closed-vocabulary supervised detectors.
Detect-anything claims fail at realistic vocabulary scale: open-vocabulary detection quality degrades systematically as the query vocabulary grows toward thousands of concurrent names.
Per-class score incomparability breaks open-vocabulary deployment: a single global confidence threshold is near-meaningless because score distributions differ arbitrarily across queried names.

A scene-prior skyline exposes benchmark weakness: an image-level classifier plus class-agnostic proposals matches open-vocabulary detectors on a large share of benchmark classes without any region-text alignment.
IoU is the wrong metric below a size threshold: center-distance-based matching reorders small-object detection methods and agrees better with human quality judgments.

Sub-pixel translation reveals stride aliasing: small-object detection output oscillates strongly under tiny image shifts because object size interacts with feature stride, a deterministic and fixable artifact.

Image-level foundation pretraining is a poor donor for small-dense detection: at matched compute, dense-prediction-oriented pretraining beats caption or image-level contrastive pretraining specifically on the small and dense stratum.
NMS makes detection-based counting undercount predictably in dense scenes: there is a characterizable density crossover beyond which suppression errors dominate and density-map methods win.

Most claimed small-object method gains are pixel-budget effects: at equal effective input pixels on the object, specialized small-object techniques lose most of their advantage over plain high-resolution inference.

Tiny-object classification is contextual inference, not appearance recognition: below a resolvable size, detectors name objects from scene context, and context-swap tests expose this hidden dependence.
Dense-scene errors are dominated by duplicate and merge mistakes that AP barely registers: a dedicated identity-error metric reveals a failure axis invisible in current rankings.

Fixed query budgets create a silent recall cliff: query-based detectors fail abruptly when instance count approaches the query count, and the failure is invisible on benchmarks dominated by sparse images.
Benchmark-defined small is not domain small: small-object method rankings established on natural-photo benchmarks invert on scale distributions typical of aerial or microscopy imagery.

Training assignment starves tiny objects: standard positive-sample assignment gives near-zero learning signal to the smallest objects, and oracle-assignment experiments would recover much of the small-object gap.

Size priming in detection: small instances are found mainly when larger same-class instances co-occur in the image, and isolated small objects fail disproportionately, a bias hidden by co-occurrence-heavy benchmarks.
Detectors hallucinate regularity in packed layouts: on grids of repeated identical objects, models fill in missing items at empty positions, revealing pattern-completion behavior in dense detection.
Super-resolution preprocessing for small-object detection trades localization gains for classification bias: generative upsampling drags tiny-object labels toward visually typical categories.
Long-tail detection gains from reweighting losses are mostly post-hoc calibration in disguise: per-class score recalibration of a plain baseline recovers the bulk of reported rare-class improvements.
Rare-class AP is statistically vacuous at current test sizes: bootstrap confidence intervals on tail-class AP dwarf typical method gaps, so many long-tail leaderboard conclusions are noise.
Web pretraining displaces rather than solves the long tail: per-class gains from vision-language pretraining track web caption frequency, leaving web-rare classes as badly off as before.
Long-tail methods overfit the benchmark's frequency histogram: retesting under resampled tail shapes reveals that gains are tied to one particular class-frequency profile.

Tail classes are recognized by their habitats: rare-class detection succeeds mainly in stereotyped contexts, and out-of-context rare instances fail at much higher rates than out-of-context common ones.
Most tail-class failure is naming, not missing: hierarchical evaluation that credits superclass-correct detections reveals the long-tail gap is largely a fine-grained labeling gap.
Copy-paste augmentation teaches paste detection: rare-class gains from copy-paste partly reflect boundary and compositing cues, and artifact-free insertion tests would show smaller true gains.

Repeat-factor sampling helps through contexts, not instances: oversampling images containing rare classes mostly benefits by re-exposing their scene contexts, which context-only controls can demonstrate.
Average tail AP hides intra-tail regression: long-tail methods improve some rare classes while actively degrading others, and worst-group reporting would change which methods look best.

The tail gap decomposes into proposal recall versus classification differently than assumed: for unusual-shaped rare objects the real bottleneck is objectness transfer, not naming, inverting the standard decomposition.
Boxes already contain masks: frozen features of box-only detectors support high-quality mask prediction with tiny mask supervision, suggesting mask annotation budgets are largely wasted.

Segmentation-first detection wins on irregular objects: deriving boxes from class-agnostic masks beats box-first pipelines for thin, curved, and perforated objects, an advantage hidden by benchmark shape statistics.

Interior-dominated mask metrics hide boundary failure: instance segmentation progress measured by mask IoU has plateaued at boundaries, and boundary-weighted evaluation reorders methods and better predicts downstream utility.

Detector-to-segmenter pipelines fail multiplicatively, not independently: promptable segmenters amplify detector box errors on exactly the hard instances, so pipeline quality is worse than the product of component qualities.

Amodal-modal convention mismatch breaks detection-segmentation stacks under occlusion: components trained with different visibility conventions disagree precisely on occluded objects, and pipelines silently mix the two.

Training detection through mask-derived objectives improves boxes themselves: replacing box regression targets with boxes derived from predicted masks yields better localization even measured by box AP on non-convex objects.

Instance segmentation systematically forbids nested instances: overlap-resolution heuristics assume quasi-disjoint objects, making object-inside-object cases a structural blind spot across current methods.

Detection-segmentation multitask benefit is one-directional: detection supervision helps segmentation, but segmentation supervision adds little to detection at foundation scale, contradicting the mutual-benefit narrative.
The thing-stuff boundary is a load-bearing arbitrary choice: reclassifying ambiguous categories between thing and stuff swings panoptic comparisons, so panoptic rankings partly measure ontology luck.
Segmenter stability is a better detection confidence than the detector's own score: rescoring detections by mask agreement under prompt jitter improves ranking quality without retraining anything.

Dense pretraining transfers to detection through objectness, not classification: pixel-level pretraining gains concentrate in proposal recall, implying cheap class-agnostic dense objectives could replace expensive semantic ones.
Attribute binding fails at the instance level in open-vocabulary detection: with two objects of swapped attributes in one scene, detectors match queries to the wrong instances at near-chance rates.

Web-pretrained detectors hallucinate companion objects: scores for typically co-occurring categories are elevated even when absent, and this co-occurrence hallucination exceeds that of in-domain supervised detectors.
Typographic attacks transfer from classification to open-vocabulary detection: text written in the scene shifts region scores, so rendered words act as adversarial detection evidence.

Foundation detector errors are correlated across model families: shared web data induces shared blind spots, so ensembling different foundation detectors yields far less error diversity than their architectural diversity suggests.

Foundation detectors have a canonical-scale prior: objects photographed at atypical absolute scales, extreme close-ups or extreme distance, are missed in ways predicted by web photo composition statistics, and rescaling recovers them.

Foundation detectors are right for the wrong pixels: attribution analysis shows their class decisions rely on context outside the box far more than supervised detectors, predicting brittleness that in-box-only evaluation misses.

Frozen foundation features hit a localization precision ceiling: high-IoU detection quality saturates regardless of head capacity, because image-level pretraining discards sub-patch spatial precision that fine-tuning must rebuild.

Foundation detectors have a web-aesthetic prior: semantically harmless but statistically atypical imaging conditions, unusual white balance, nonstandard aspect ratios, flash artifacts, degrade them more than matched supervised detectors.

Multimodal LLMs are better detection verifiers than detectors: their box generation fails on coordinate production, not perception, so the generation-verification gap argues for verifier-role deployment.

Multimodal LLM boxes betray tokenizer priors: generated coordinates cluster on round numbers and canonical aspect ratios, a measurable output-distribution distortion that standard AP evaluation never reveals.

Caption-worthiness bias shapes foundation detection: recall as a function of object size, centrality, and photographic salience is steeper for web-pretrained detectors, penalizing peripheral and incidental objects.

Vocabulary forgetting outpaces domain gains: fine-tuning open-vocabulary detectors on narrow domains erases their broad-vocabulary competence at a rate that makes naive domain adaptation a net capability loss.
State breaks detectors before category does: foundation detectors fail on known objects in unusual states, overturned, disassembled, damaged, more than on unseen categories in canonical states.
Foundation detectors cannot say this image is not for me: on out-of-scope imagery they emit confident structured detections instead of abstaining, and no standard evaluation measures scope awareness.
At foundation scale, detection error is almost all recognition: class-agnostic localization is near ceiling, so architecture work on box mechanisms attacks a solved subproblem.
Localization and recognition want incompatible features: two-stream detectors reading separate frozen representations for where and what beat single-feature detectors at matched compute.

IoU-threshold sweeps fingerprint what a method actually improved: most claimed detection advances are either pure-recognition or pure-localization gains, and the sweep signature exposes mislabeled contributions.
Detectors should output box uncertainty, not just label confidence: cheap per-coordinate uncertainty adds little AP but transforms downstream decision quality, exposing a metric-deployment mismatch.

Extent errors, not center errors, dominate the high-IoU regime, and they trace to annotation-convention ambiguity about what counts as the object, handles, shadows, occluded parts, rather than to model weakness.

Detection classification is not crop classification: region labels depend on an optimal, class-specific amount of context, and both context-free crops and whole-image reasoning underperform the learned intermediate.

Objectness saturates early while recognition keeps scaling: detection-specific pretraining spends compute on a subskill that stops improving, arguing for classification-heavy pretraining plus minimal localization adaptation.

Duplicate suppression is a recognition problem misassigned to geometry: identity-aware deduplication that asks are these the same object beats overlap-threshold suppression exactly where detection is hardest, adjacent identical objects.

A scene-statistics decision rule for counting: measurable image properties predict whether detection-based or regression-based counting will be more accurate on a given image, enabling per-image method routing.

Multimodal LLM counting is subitizing plus guessing: exact counting holds up to a small integer and then collapses to density-conditioned estimation, a signature invisible in benchmarks that average over count ranges.

Crowding suppresses per-instance recall independent of resolution: detection probability of an instance declines with the number of identical neighbors even when size and image quality are held constant.

Counts are cheap detection supervision: adding per-image count labels for classes without box annotations improves detection of those classes, unlocking abundant inventory-style metadata as training signal.
Detector-regressor disagreement finds annotation errors: images where detection-based and density-based counts diverge are enriched for ground-truth mistakes, yielding a free annotation-audit signal.

Partial-visibility conventions drive counting disagreement: a large share of counting error concentrates on instances whose countability is convention-ambiguous, edge-cropped, mostly occluded, or reflected objects.

Class-averaged detection AP is driven by a volatile minority: bootstrap analysis shows overall benchmark rankings hinge on a handful of high-variance classes, making leaderboard stability an illusion.
AP rewards unusable predictions: methods gain benchmark points from dense low-confidence box floods that no deployment threshold would keep, so operating-point metrics reorder detection leaderboards.

Detection test sets are effectively smaller than they look: image-level and instance-level near-duplicates inflate effective sample size, understating uncertainty and overstating fine-grained method distinctions.

The default detection-count cap censors dense scenes: standard evaluation truncates predictions per image at a fixed limit, so performance on the densest images is systematically unmeasured and methods are blind-ranked there.

Greedy confidence-ordered matching biases AP against certain prediction styles: optimal-assignment scoring changes per-method AP unevenly, revealing that part of measured differences is matching-algorithm artifact.
Unreported inference-time enhancements account for a large share of detection leaderboard deltas: equal-inference-budget re-evaluation collapses many claimed architecture advantages.

Benchmark precision is annotation-limited for top detectors: a substantial share of their scored false positives are correct detections of unannotated objects, so measured precision differences among strong models are annotation artifacts.

Annotation conventions drift within datasets: box tightness and part-inclusion practices vary across annotation batches, and detectors learn the average, producing systematic per-batch evaluation bias.

Granularity-ambiguous aggregates drive outsized detection error: stacks, piles, and clusters annotated inconsistently as one-or-many account for a disproportionate share of both false positives and misses.

High-IoU evaluation operates beyond the human agreement floor: inter-annotator box IoU distributions show that strict-threshold metrics score models against noise, and noise-floor-normalized metrics change conclusions.

Detectors out-localize their own training labels: model predictions are systematically closer to multi-annotator consensus than the single-annotator boxes they were trained and evaluated on, so evaluation penalizes models for being right.

Model confusion matrices partially replicate annotator confusion: class-label errors in detection datasets are structured by visual similarity and annotation workflow, and models inherit these exact confusions, inflating measured semantic error.

Sparse-annotation training teaches contextual self-censorship: detectors trained under incomplete labeling learn context-dependent suppression of valid detections, producing deployment blind spots that complete-annotation fine-tuning reverses.

The last transformer layer of contrastively pretrained vision-language models is systematically the worst layer for dense language alignment, because global-pooling pressure concentrates text alignment in summary tokens at the expense of patch tokens.

Open-vocabulary segmentation leaderboards measure mask-proposal quality, not language grounding: swapping the text encoder barely moves scores while swapping the class-agnostic mask generator moves them dramatically.
Two-stage segment-then-classify pipelines are structurally biased against stuff categories because cropping a region for classification destroys exactly the context that defines stuff.

Training-free attention-surgery methods for dense CLIP-style inference gain mostly by spatially denoising features, and simple spatial smoothing of unmodified features recovers much of their improvement.
Text-to-patch similarity maps in contrastive VLMs localize by visual salience rather than by language: irrelevant text queries still highlight the same salient object.
Class-agnostic mask generators impose a granularity prior that mismatches linguistic category boundaries, capping open-vocabulary segmentation regardless of grounding quality.

Dense language-grounding quality scales with caption richness (words and noun phrases per image) rather than raw pair count, making data curation for dense tasks orthogonal to curation for classification.

Retrieval-based dense labeling, transferring labels from retrieved segmented neighbors in frozen VLM feature space, can rival learned open-vocabulary segmentation heads while being training-free and instantly extensible.

Language-grounded segmenters lean on scene-context correlations so strongly that they segment object regions correctly even when the object itself is erased, revealing context-driven rather than evidence-driven masks.

Prompt ensembling, a free win for zero-shot classification, is a mixed blessing for dense prediction: it helps region interiors but systematically blurs boundaries by averaging spatially incompatible similarity maps.

Fine-tuning VLMs on segmentation data narrows the open vocabulary at pixel level much faster than at image level, so standard image-level forgetting checks certify models that have already lost dense open-vocabulary ability.
Referring expression segmentation benchmarks are largely solvable by detecting the head noun and picking the most salient instance, so reported scores overstate relational language understanding.

Referring models fail to ground text-dependent references (objects identified by written labels in the image) even when the same system reads that text correctly in a question-answering mode, revealing an OCR-grounding integration gap.
No-target referring, correctly refusing to segment when the expression matches nothing, is the dominant unsolved failure mode: models confidently produce masks for absent referents.
Multi-target and exception referring expressions break single-instance architectural priors: models emit exactly one mask because their decoders structurally assume one referent.
Round-trip referring, where a model generates an expression for a region and then must comprehend its own expression, exposes grounding gaps invisible to standard one-way evaluation.
Referring segmentation built on multimodal LLMs is bottlenecked by vision-encoder resolution, not language reasoning: failures concentrate on small referents regardless of expression clarity.

Referring models fail on novel attribute-object combinations at segmentation time even when both the attribute and the object are individually well-grounded, exposing missing compositional binding in dense grounding.

Contrastive pretraining's learned temperature makes pixel-level similarity scores relative rankings rather than probabilities, so open-set pixel calibration requires anchoring scores to an absolute alignment reference.

Vocabulary-granularity mismatch is a dominant unmeasured error source: models are marked wrong for answering at a different but correct level of the concept hierarchy, and hierarchy-aware scoring reranks methods.

Synonym inconsistency is a cheap unforgiving audit: querying the same class by different correct names yields materially different masks, and consistency across synonyms could be enforced as a free constraint.

Rare-class pixel labeling is governed by name statistics rather than visual difficulty: classes with common visual appearance but rare names underperform classes with rare appearance but common names.

Unseen-category generalization claims in open-vocabulary segmentation are inflated because unseen classes are visually near seen ones; stratifying by visual distance to the seen set reveals sharply weaker true generalization.

Anomaly segmentation via abstract text queries fails because contrastive text encoders cannot ground non-referential language: queries like unusual or out-of-place behave as near-noise directions in alignment space.

Open-vocabulary segmentation degradation in specialist domains is driven more by the text tower than the vision tower: domain terms are poorly embedded, and text-side interventions recover more than image-side ones.

Scaling the query vocabulary to encyclopedic size produces confusion patterns predictable from text-embedding neighborhoods alone, enabling a text-only forecast of dense failure before running any image.

VLM patch features lack mid-range context integration: they are simultaneously too global for instance boundaries and too local for stuff coherence, and the missing scale is measurable and fixable at inference.

Resolution-scaling tricks for dense inference silently corrupt text alignment: interpolating position embeddings improves geometry while drifting patch features away from the text tower's expected distribution.
Sliding-window dense inference produces label inconsistencies for the same object across windows, and lightweight global conditioning eliminates a class of errors that post-hoc blending merely hides.
Anisotropy of contrastive patch embeddings makes cosine similarity a low-information ranking signal densely, and simple whitening of patch features reorders and improves pixel-label decisions.

Multimodal LLMs contain more spatial detail than their language outputs use: pixel-probing their vision features beats their own verbalized dense answers, locating dense failure at the interface rather than in perception.

Segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs hallucinate masks for absent objects at rates far exceeding their question-answering hallucination rates, making dense hallucination the field's most undermeasured risk.

Language-grounded segmenters are internally inconsistent about amodal versus modal extent: whether occluded object parts are included depends on the query phrasing and the occluder's category, not on any coherent convention.

Aspect-ratio deviation from pretraining crops damages dense predictions much more than global ones: padding, squeezing, and tiling choices at inference are a silent variance source dense benchmarks never control.

Template context words in prompts spatially bias dense predictions: boundary pixels are more sensitive to prompt wording than interior pixels, so prompt choice partially determines boundary placement.

The best-aligned layer for dense prediction differs systematically by query type (things versus stuff, objects versus parts), so any single-layer feature choice is guaranteed suboptimal and query-adaptive layer selection is free accuracy.

The confusion matrix of an open-vocabulary segmenter is largely predictable from text-encoder geometry alone, before any image is processed, making text-side audits a cheap proxy for dense error analysis.

Hub class names, text embeddings abnormally close to many patch features, absorb pixels from many true classes, and hubness-correction techniques from retrieval transfer directly to dense labeling as training-free gains.

Class-name token length biases dense similarity magnitudes, so multi-word categories are systematically under- or over-predicted, and length normalization is a missing preprocessing step in every open-vocabulary pipeline.
Polysemous class names produce sense-blended text embeddings that corrupt dense predictions, and sense-disambiguating prompt contexts recover accuracy on quietly polysemous benchmark classes.

Contrastive text encoders barely encode spatial-relational words: removing them from referring expressions leaves the text embedding nearly unchanged, mechanistically explaining relation-blind dense grounding.

Negation invariance of contrastive text embeddings transfers directly into dense prediction: negated queries produce near-identical similarity maps to affirmative ones, and the embedding distance between a phrase and its negation predicts which models can be fixed by prompting alone.

Attribute-binding failure is text-side measurable: swapped-attribute expressions embed nearly identically in contrastive towers, and this bag-of-words geometry upper-bounds dense binding accuracy no matter how good the vision tower is.
Cross-lingual dense inconsistency, where translated class names yield different masks on the same image, is large, systematic, and a free multilingual audit for text-tower quality in dense pipelines.

Dense grounding models resolve frame-of-reference ambiguity by always choosing the viewer-centric reading, and benchmarks silently reward this because annotators did too, hiding a genuine ambiguity the field has never measured.

Dense grounding handles canonical categorical relations but fails graded and metric spatial language: nearest, halfway, and almost-touching ground at near-chance despite high scores on left-right-above benchmarks.
Relational grounding accuracy decays superlinearly with scene clutter because models approximate relations with global position priors that collapse when many candidates occupy every image region.

Depth-dependent relations fail because VLM features encode little metric depth, and supplying monocular depth as an auxiliary input disproportionately repairs behind and in-front-of while leaving 2D relations unchanged, cleanly attributing the failure.

Relative-size references ground by image-plane area rather than real-world size: models pick the object with more pixels, failing whenever perspective makes the physically larger object smaller in the frame.

Dense grounding models trained on web photos fail systematically on egocentric viewpoints, and the failure is viewpoint-distributional rather than object-level: the same objects ground fine in third-person views.

Grounding accuracy decays multiplicatively per relational hop in nested expressions, and measuring the per-hop decay factor gives a single scalar that predicts model behavior on arbitrarily complex referring chains.

Spatial terms function as tie-breakers, not constraints: models first shortlist referents by appearance and only consult spatial language when appearance ties, an order of operations exposable by appearance-spatial conflict stimuli.

Cross-dataset open-vocabulary evaluation partially measures label-name compatibility: renaming target-dataset classes to equally correct synonyms reranks methods, revealing name-matching as a hidden score component.
Referring benchmarks contain enough annotation ambiguity that top models may already be at the inter-annotator ceiling, making current leaderboard differences unmeasurable noise.

Background-region conventions are inconsistent across dense benchmarks and methods, and harmonizing background handling alone shifts reported open-vocabulary gaps enough to change some published conclusions.

A query-in-the-wild protocol, evaluating dense models on free-form user queries collected without benchmark vocabulary constraints, would reveal a large gap between benchmark scores and experienced quality.

Self-training with VLM-generated pseudo-masks amplifies text-side biases round over round: classes favored by text geometry gain pixels each iteration, and the drift is measurable, predictable, and correctable with text-side debiasing.

The missing dense alignment in contrastive VLMs is a shallow, learnable transform: a small frozen-backbone decoder trained on limited data recovers most of the gap to full fine-tuning, showing the information was present but misformatted.

Patch-level contrastive alignment objectives are ill-posed at boundaries because patches straddle classes, and boundary-aware assignment during training removes a systematic soft-boundary artifact that plagues all patch-supervised dense models.

Fine-tuning the text tower for dense tasks is more damaging to open-vocabulary ability than fine-tuning the vision tower: alignment forgetting is asymmetric across towers, and freezing choice should follow the asymmetry.

Training dense models on synthetic captions transfers the captioner's blind spots as a hard ceiling: student dense performance per concept is bounded by the teacher captioner's mention behavior, creating invisible inherited gaps.

Mixing instance-mask and semantic-mask supervision teaches conflicting notions of object extent, and the conflict measurably hurts referring tasks that need instances, suggesting supervision-type should be conditioned, not pooled.

Part queries retrieve wholes: language-grounded segmenters asked for object parts return whole-object masks because caption supervision represents parts as attributes of wholes rather than as spatial units.

Natural-language granularity cues (the whole X, just the Y of the X) fail to control mask extent reliably, while an explicit granularity token interface succeeds, showing granularity is representable but not language-accessible.
Predicted part and whole masks violate containment at high rates, and enforcing part-whole consistency at inference is a free accuracy and trustworthiness gain no current system exploits.

Open-vocabulary segmenters exhibit basic-level bias: superordinate queries like animal produce worse masks than basic-level names for the same regions, because caption language overwhelmingly uses basic-level terms.

Stuff-stuff boundary placement is learned as dataset convention, not visual inference: models transfer their training dataset's boundary style to new domains, and cross-dataset boundary disagreement quantifies this hidden convention learning.

Linguistic countability drives segmentation topology: mass-noun phrasing yields merged regions and count-noun phrasing yields instance-like masks for the same visual material, an unmeasured coupling between grammar and mask structure.

Ordinal reference (the second cup from the left) grounds at near-chance across dense models because ordinal computation requires an explicit sort the architectures never perform, and errors follow a predictable off-by-adjacency pattern.

Instance counts derived from language-grounded segmentation systematically undercount in crowded scenes with a density-dependent bias, and the bias curve is stable enough to invert for calibrated counting.

Complement queries (everything except the sky) fail despite being trivially computable from the affirmative mask, exposing that dense systems lack a negation-as-set-operation pathway even where no perception is required.

Attribute-only queries (everything red) are object-mediated: models find red objects but miss red stuff and red object-parts, revealing that attributes are grounded through object nouns rather than as pixel properties.

Dense systems treat conjunctive and disjunctive queries identically: cats and dogs versus cats or dogs produce indistinguishable masks, revealing that logical connectives are dropped at the grounding interface.

Metric-quantitative spatial queries (objects larger than half the image, within ten pixels of the border) are wholly ungrounded in dense systems, and their failure profile shows quantities are parsed as vague intensifiers.

State-conditioned queries (the open door, the empty cup) lag object queries by a wide margin at dense level, and the gap measures a state-grounding deficit distinct from object recognition that paired-state scenes isolate cleanly.

Segmentation tokens in multimodal LLMs are a low-bandwidth bottleneck: mask fidelity saturates with the information capacity of the token embedding, measurable by comparing token-decoded masks against directly decoded masks from the same visual features.

Autoregressive coordinate emission for dense outputs accumulates spatial error along the sequence: later polygon vertices and later boxes in a list are systematically less accurate, an interface artifact invisible to aggregate metrics.

Chain-of-thought reasoning before mask emission can hurt grounding: reasoning tokens displace visual attention, and mask accuracy on perceptually easy targets drops when models are made to think longer.

Multimodal LLMs are dense-inconsistent across query formats: pointing at a pixel and asking what it is contradicts asking where a named thing is, and cross-format agreement is a label-free quality audit plus a constraint for free improvement.

Segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs cannot express spatial uncertainty: their verbalized doubts about mask regions are uncorrelated with actual boundary errors, leaving dense outputs without any usable confidence channel.

Multi-turn mask correction fails because dialog context does not effectively carry mask state: models treat each correction as a fresh query, and correction success barely exceeds single-turn retry rates.

Visual prompt overlays (marks, boxes, highlights drawn on the image) contaminate the visual stream: they alter dense predictions for unmarked objects, an interference effect that mark-based prompting studies never control.

High-resolution tiling strategies for multimodal LLMs improve text-reading tasks far more than segmentation because cross-tile attention fails to reintegrate object geometry, producing task-dependent resolution scaling that current unified benchmarks average away.
Synthetic-data gains in semantic segmentation concentrate on boundary and thin-structure pixels, so pixel-perfect labels rather than scene realism are the active ingredient.
Mixing pixel-perfect synthetic labels with convention-noisy human labels creates conflicting supervision that caps segmentation performance, and harmonizing label conventions recovers the loss.

Optical flow transfer from synthetic training data is governed by motion statistics rather than photorealism, so matching real motion distributions with crude rendering beats photorealistic data with mismatched motion.
For object detection, cut-and-paste composition with mediocre blending matches full 3D rendering pipelines once a low realism threshold is passed, making blending quality an over-optimized axis.

The value of synthetic data per task is predicted by the cost of acquiring real labels for that task, not by the size of the domain gap, revealing label scarcity rather than realism as the binding constraint.
Synthetic scene generators systematically under-produce heavy-occlusion configurations, and matching real occlusion statistics yields more detection and segmentation transfer than improving textures.
For human pose estimation, sampling synthetic poses approximately uniformly over kinematically valid space transfers better than sampling from realistic motion-capture distributions.
Synthetic stuff classes transfer nearly for free while thing classes carry most of the sim-to-real gap, motivating hybrid pipelines that render backgrounds and paste real object instances.
Synthetic video with perfectly coherent frames teaches temporal over-smoothness, so video models trained on it degrade on real footage with cuts, jitter, and exposure changes.

Reconstructing real scenes into neural 3D representations and re-rendering them with perturbed cameras yields dense supervision with real appearance, and this real2sim2real data beats graphics rendering for dense tasks.
Domain randomization mostly re-implements strong 2D augmentation, and equally aggressive augmentation of a small real set matches heavy randomization in simulation for many perception tasks.
Foundation-model backbones have made photorealism largely obsolete for sim-to-real: with frozen pretrained features, low-fidelity rendering transfers as well as high-fidelity rendering.
The direction and size of the sim-real transfer asymmetry (sim-to-real versus real-to-sim) is a cheap diagnostic that identifies whether a gap is appearance-driven or content-driven.

Models exploit renderer-specific spectral and noise signatures as shortcuts, and matching low-level image statistics between synthetic and real data removes a large, cheap-to-fix share of the sim-to-real gap.
Sim-to-real adaptation method rankings established on driving benchmarks do not transfer to other target domains, making the canonical leaderboard a domain artifact.
Adapting label-space statistics (class frequencies, object size and count distributions) via resampling beats image-space adaptation for sim-to-real transfer at a fraction of the cost.
For contact-rich robotic perception, physics fidelity dominates visual fidelity in sim-to-real transfer, inverting the effort allocation of typical simulation pipelines.

Generative image translation of synthetic frames corrupts dense labels by hallucinating and deleting content, so translation-based sim-to-real gains are overstated for dense tasks and label-corruption audits should be mandatory.
Weather and lighting randomization in driving simulation covers a thin manifold of real conditions, and a nearest-neighbor coverage audit predicts per-condition transfer failure before any training.
Pixel-perfect synthetic labels can transfer worse than convention-matched noisy labels because evaluation rewards agreement with human annotator behavior, not with geometric truth.

Foundation-model pseudo-labels carry attribute-correlated structured noise, so noise-robust learning methods validated on uniform synthetic noise fail on the auto-label noise that actually matters now.
Boundary-localized label noise damages segmentation training far more per pixel than interior noise, and a boundary-weighted noise metric predicts downstream harm where raw noise rate fails.

Auto-label noise correlates with example difficulty, so confidence-based label cleaning preferentially deletes hard examples and produces models that score better on clean averages but worse on hard tails.
Beyond a threshold noise level, a small verified-clean validation set is worth more per annotation dollar than any quantity of additional noisy training labels, and the exchange rate is measurable.
Confidence-based label cleaning entrenches the teacher's biases in the student: samples where the teacher is confidently wrong survive cleaning, creating a measurable self-confirmation loop.

The soft-versus-hard pseudo-label debate reduces to teacher calibration: soft labels win with calibrated teachers and lose with miscalibrated ones, and a calibration measurement predicts the winner per setup.

Most of what is booked as label noise in dense annotation is actually irreducible instruction ambiguity, and synthetic data with a single rendering convention trains models to be confidently wrong about genuinely ambiguous pixels.

Missing-annotation noise (unlabeled true objects treated as background) dominates wrong-label noise in detection training, and exhaustively labeled synthetic data makes the resulting precision-recall distortion worse, not better.
Synthetic-data quality filters are task-anticorrelated: filters tuned for classification-style aesthetics remove exactly the cluttered, occluded, hard scenes that dense tasks need most.

The training value of a synthetic sample is predictable at generation time from generator-internal signals, enabling curation before rendering and saving most of the generation compute that post-hoc filtering wastes.

Embedding-coverage diversity metrics saturate long before task utility does, and compositional attribute diversity keeps paying after coverage metrics flatline, exposing a blind spot in curation dashboards.

For low-resource target domains, curating real web data to match a synthetic reference distribution beats curating synthetic data to match limited real samples, reversing the standard curation direction.
Difficulty-based hard-example mining on synthetic pools preferentially selects generator failure artifacts rather than genuinely hard content, actively injecting shortcut features into training.

Data-pruning conclusions invert with scale on synthetic pools: pruning helps at small training budgets and hurts at large ones, with a predictable crossover that current papers ignore by evaluating at single scales.
The optimal real-to-synthetic mixing ratio is predictable from gradient alignment between real and synthetic mini-batches measured early in training, eliminating expensive mixing-ratio sweeps.

Cross-boundary deduplication between synthetic pools and real train and test sets is a missing pipeline stage: synthetic near-duplicates of test data inflate benchmarks and near-duplicates of train data add nothing.
Source-level scheduling (synthetic-then-real annealing) dominates example-level curriculum within synthetic data, so curation effort spent ordering synthetic examples is largely wasted.

Influence-style valuation against a real validation set reveals that most of a typical synthetic pool has near-zero or negative training value, with the positive value concentrated in a small identifiable slice.

Generative synthetic-data utility scales with distinct-prompt count, not image count: images-per-prompt beyond a small number is nearly wasted compute, making prompt engineering the real dataset-size lever.

Procedural and abstract-image pretraining works by installing generic early-layer filters, so its benefit saturates at small scale and vanishes for foundation-scale models with long real-data training.
Training students on generator-produced data is distillation, not discovery: it accelerates learning toward the generator's knowledge but cannot exceed it, and the ceiling is measurable.

Synthetic data helps foundation models where real data is thin: a density-targeted synthesis policy that generates in low-density regions of the real distribution beats uniform synthesis at equal budget.
Synthetic captions improve benchmark retrieval scores while quietly degrading robustness under distribution shift because they homogenize the text distribution that contrastive training consumes.
Rendering-based synthetic pretraining transfers to geometry-loaded tasks and not to semantics-loaded ones, and a task's geometry-semantics loading predicts its synthetic-pretraining benefit.
The real-data fraction needed to anchor mostly-synthetic pretraining shrinks with model scale, opening a path where foundation models train predominantly on synthetic data with small real anchors.

Self-supervised objectives differ systematically in synthetic-data tolerance: reconstruction-style objectives degrade less on synthetic pretraining data than contrastive ones, so data provenance should drive objective choice.
Tagging synthetic samples with a provenance token during pretraining recovers most of the performance lost to synthetic contamination, versus silently mixing, at essentially zero cost.
Students inherit generator fingerprints from synthetic training data strongly enough that the generator identity is recoverable from student behavior, enabling training-data supply-chain forensics.

Generating training data with a large generator to train a small task model beats direct real-data training only inside a predictable regime boundary defined by the task's distance from the generator's training distribution.
Synthetic-pretraining effects survive full fine-tuning for dense tasks but wash out for classification, contradicting the belief that ample fine-tuning erases pretraining data differences uniformly.
Self-training loops plateau because of diversity collapse in what gets auto-labeled, not noise accumulation, and an entropy audit of accepted pseudo-labels predicts the plateau before it arrives.

Text-to-image augmentation gains are bounded by the generator's within-class diversity, which is far below real data, and a generator-side recall measurement predicts the augmentation ceiling per class.
Editing real images beats generating from scratch for augmentation at equal budget because edits preserve real image statistics while still adding controlled variation, especially for dense tasks.
The best use of generative models for dense tasks is generating labels for real images rather than images for synthetic labels, inverting the standard generation pipeline.

Published diffusion-augmentation gains shrink dramatically against modern strong-augmentation baselines, surviving mainly in low-data regimes, and a reproduction matrix would recalibrate the field's expectations.
Students inherit compositional failure modes of their generative teachers: training on diffusion data measurably degrades counting and structural accuracy relative to matched real-data training.

Web-crawl vintages carry rising synthetic fractions, and models pretrained on different crawl vintages show behavior drift attributable to synthetic contamination, making vintage a measurable data-quality variable.

Bilevel-optimal data generation (generate to directly maximize student validation improvement) is approximable by first-order gradient matching at a tiny fraction of the cost, capturing most of its gain.

Deliberately generating realistic near-miss hard negatives improves fine-grained discrimination more than generating additional positives, making negative synthesis the underused half of generative augmentation.

Generated video is a poor training source for temporal representations because its artifacts are temporal, and hybrid data (generated appearance with real motion) beats end-to-end video generation for training video models.
Transfer from graphics data scales with distinct 3D asset count without saturating, while realism knobs saturate early, so generation budgets should buy assets, not rendering quality.

A procedurally infinite stream of moderate-quality scenes beats any fixed-size high-quality synthetic dataset for dense tasks, because non-repetition eliminates the synthetic-overfitting failure mode.
Renderer identity leaves shortcut fingerprints that models exploit, and mixing multiple renderers is a near-free domain-randomization axis stronger than texture randomization.

Tasks defined only through synthetic supervision, like intrinsic decomposition, may have models that learned renderer conventions rather than physics, and a real-light-transport audit would expose the gap.
Layout realism (object co-occurrence and physical support relations) transfers more than appearance realism, so scene-grammar investment beats shading investment at equal cost.
Procedural generation parameters can be optimized directly against downstream validation performance with black-box methods, because the loss over generation parameters is smoother than assumed.
Rendered-human training data shows an uncanny-valley non-monotonicity: mid-realism renders transfer worse than either stylized or high-realism renders for person-centric tasks.

Generator quality metrics like distribution-distance scores are nearly uncorrelated with the training utility of generated data, and the field needs utility-specific metrics rather than borrowed perceptual ones.

Train-on-synthetic-test-on-real rankings of synthetic datasets flip across student architectures, so dataset-superiority claims made with one architecture are architecture-conditional statements in disguise.
A cheap probe suite over frozen foundation features can predict the full-training utility of a synthetic dataset, replacing most train-to-evaluate cycles in curation loops.

Synthetic test sets systematically compress model rankings because generators regress toward typical instances, making synthetic evaluation optimistically biased and rank-unstable for model comparison.
Synthetic data quality is two independent axes, fidelity and coverage, that trade off differently per task, and single-scalar quality reporting systematically misleads adoption decisions.

Generators have seen the benchmarks: synthetic training data leaks evaluation content through generator memorization, inflating synthetic-data results in ways standard contamination checks never audit.
Reported synthetic-data gains are confounded by asymmetric tuning effort, and equal-tuning-budget re-evaluation would deflate a measurable share of published improvements.

Per-image accounting hides the cost of synthetic data: under per-FLOP accounting that includes generation compute, many synthetic-data results are net-negative versus simply training longer on real data.
Batch-generated synthetic data violates the i.i.d. assumption through shared seeds, prompts, and scheduler state, and decorrelating generation batches yields free training gains.

Renderer labels are not ground truth for the evaluation convention: anti-aliased boundaries, transparency, and reflections are labeled by renderer logic that systematically disagrees with human annotation guidelines.
More realism is not monotonically better: past a threshold, realistic synthesis re-imports the real world's spurious correlations that cruder randomized data had removed, hurting robustness.

Synthetic data optimized to match today's distribution is optimized for the wrong target when deployment shifts the distribution, and shift-anticipating synthesis beats distribution-matching synthesis.
Synthetic data is assumed privacy-safe by construction, but generator memorization leaks training individuals, and the utility cost of verified non-memorization is unknown and possibly severe.
The domain gap is treated as a scalar when it is a decomposable vector over appearance, content, sensor, and label-convention factors, and interventions are systematically misattributed as a result.

Generation vintage is a hidden curriculum: synthetic corpora accumulate quality drift as pipelines improve, and ordering training by vintage versus shuffling changes outcomes, an unexamined degree of freedom.
The student-cannot-exceed-teacher assumption fails for dense geometry: averaging noisy generator-derived labels across many views or samples lets students surpass their labeling teacher measurably.
Real and synthetic data follow different scaling exponents that interact, and a two-term joint scaling law fitted from pilot runs predicts the optimal real-synthetic mix at any budget.
Synthetic-data returns plateau when the student saturates the generator's effective support, and the intrinsic dimension of the generated set predicts the plateau point before training reaches it.
The true unit cost of synthetic data is dominated by curation, validation, and integration rather than generation, and total-cost accounting reverses several published cost-benefit claims.
Small domain-specialized generators beat giant general generators as training-data engines at equal generation compute, contradicting the bigger-generator-is-better default.
When real data is exhausted, repeating real epochs beats adding synthetic data up to a predictable repetition count, and the repetition-versus-synthesis crossover is a fittable law.

Synthetic datasets depreciate faster than real datasets as deployment distributions and conventions drift, and measuring dataset half-life reveals different amortization economics for the two data types.
